purposes.label: Running the country
purposes.explain: Making laws, collecting taxes, keeping records, statistics and elections, and links with other countries.

purposes.label: Defence
purposes.explain: The armed forces and keeping the country safe from attack.

purposes.label: Police, courts and safety
purposes.explain: Police, fire and rescue, courts, prisons and the justice system.

purposes.label: Money, business and transport
purposes.explain: Jobs, business, trade, farming, energy, roads, railways, ports and airports.

purposes.label: Nature and the environment
purposes.explain: Protecting nature, cleaning up pollution and looking after the countryside and sea.

purposes.label: Homes and local places
purposes.explain: Housing, planning new buildings, water supply and improving towns and cities.

purposes.label: Health
purposes.explain: Hospitals, doctors, medicines and keeping people healthy.

purposes.label: Culture, sport and heritage
purposes.explain: Museums, libraries, the arts, sport, broadcasting, languages and historic places.

purposes.label: Education and research
purposes.explain: Schools, colleges, universities, exams, skills and research.

purposes.label: Benefits, pensions and care
purposes.explain: Pensions, benefits, social care and support for children, families and disabled people.

purposes.label: Many local services
purposes.explain: Councils run many local services at once: bins, roads, schools, care, libraries and planning.

purposes.label: Not yet worked out
purposes.explain: The sources don't say enough yet. You can help by sending a correction.

activities.label: Makes laws
activities.explain: A parliament, assembly or council whose members debate and pass laws, approve spending and question the government.

activities.label: Runs a government
activities.explain: Ministers and civil servants who make policy, propose laws and run the departments under them.

activities.label: Decides cases
activities.explain: Courts and tribunals that settle disputes and decide what the law means in a case.

activities.label: Sets and enforces rules
activities.explain: Licenses, registers or regulates a profession, market or activity, and can take action when rules are broken.

activities.label: Inspects and audits
activities.explain: Checks that services and public money are run properly, and reports what it finds.

activities.label: Handles complaints
activities.explain: An ombudsman or commissioner who looks into complaints and stands up for people.

activities.label: Gives expert advice
activities.explain: A committee or council of experts that advises ministers but doesn't run services.

activities.label: Gives out money
activities.explain: Pays out grants, loans or investment to other organisations or people.

activities.label: Sells goods or services
activities.explain: Earns most of its income by charging customers, like a business.

activities.label: Looks after collections and places
activities.explain: Museums, galleries, libraries, archives, parks and historic places.

activities.label: Keeps records and statistics
activities.explain: Registers, records, maps and official statistics.

activities.label: Does research
activities.explain: Science and research, in its own labs or by funding others.

activities.label: Promotes and represents
activities.explain: Promotes a place, an industry or a group of people, or speaks for them.

activities.label: Runs public services
activities.explain: Delivers services to the public directly: health, councils, benefits, policing, transport and more.

activities.label: Not yet worked out
activities.explain: The sources don't say enough yet. You can help by sending a correction.

btypes.label: Parliament or assembly
btypes.explain: Where elected (or appointed) members make laws, approve spending and question the government.

btypes.label: Government department
btypes.explain: A ministerial or non-ministerial department, or a devolved government.

btypes.label: Executive agency or part of a department
btypes.explain: Run by civil servants inside a department, with its own job to do.

btypes.label: Arm's-length public body
btypes.explain: Set up by law or by ministers to work at arm's length: an executive or advisory non-departmental public body, or another statutory body.

btypes.label: Court or tribunal
btypes.explain: Where judges and tribunal members decide cases.

btypes.label: Public corporation or government company
btypes.explain: Owned or controlled by government and run like a business (ONS: public corporation).

btypes.label: NHS body
btypes.explain: A hospital trust, health board, care board or other NHS organisation.

btypes.label: Council or local public body
btypes.explain: An elected council, a group of councils, or a body that councils control.

btypes.label: Other central government body
btypes.explain: A body ONS counts as central government that doesn't fit the groups above.

btypes.label: Charity or non-profit
btypes.explain: A non-profit body that government partly funds or controls.

btypes.label: Pension scheme
btypes.explain: A pension scheme for people who worked in public services.

btypes.label: Territory or dependency
btypes.explain: An overseas territory or Crown dependency with its own government.

council-EN.label: Elected by local voters
council-EN.how_often: Every 4 years. Some councils elect all councillors at once; others elect a third or half at a time, so there is a vote in most years.
council-EN.process: Voters choose councillors for their area. The candidate with the most votes wins (first past the post). Councillors then choose a leader and cabinet; the 2026 Act stops councils choosing the older committee system. In 21 areas, councils are being replaced by new single councils (see local government reorganisation).

sources.title: GOV.UK: voting systems in local elections
Written statement: ending the committee system

council-WA.label: Elected by local voters
council-WA.process: Voters choose councillors for their area. Most councils use first past the post; the law lets a council choose ranked voting instead.

sources.title: GOV.UK: voting systems in local elections
Local Government and Elections (Wales) Act 2021, sections 14 to 16

council-SC.label: Elected by local voters
council-SC.process: Voters rank candidates in order of preference (single transferable vote), and several councillors are chosen for each area.

sources.title: GOV.UK: voting systems in local elections

council-NI.label: Elected by local voters
council-NI.process: Voters rank candidates in order of preference (single transferable vote), and several councillors are chosen for each area.

sources.title: GOV.UK: voting systems in local elections

dept-UK.label: Led by elected politicians
dept-UK.how_often: Changes after a general election (at least every 5 years) or when ministers are moved.
dept-UK.process: Ministers are chosen by the Prime Minister from the elected House of Commons or the appointed House of Lords. Civil servants, who are not elected, do the day-to-day work.

sources.title: Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022, section 4

dept-SC.label: Led by elected politicians
dept-SC.how_often: Changes after a Scottish Parliament election (every 5 years) or when ministers are moved.
dept-SC.process: The First Minister is chosen by the elected Scottish Parliament and picks the other ministers.

dept-WA.label: Led by elected politicians
dept-WA.how_often: Changes after a Senedd election (every 4 years from 2026) or when ministers are moved.
dept-WA.process: The First Minister is chosen by the elected Senedd and picks the other ministers.

dept-NI.label: Led by elected politicians
dept-NI.how_often: Changes after a Northern Ireland Assembly election (every 5 years).
dept-NI.process: Ministers come from the elected Assembly. Parties share the posts by their number of seats, and the First Minister and deputy First Minister share power.

nmd.label: Led by officials, not ministers
nmd.how_often: Leaders are appointed for a fixed term.
nmd.process: Its head or board is appointed, often after an open competition, so it can work independently of politicians. It answers to Parliament.

agency.label: Part of a government department
agency.how_often: Its chief executive is appointed when the post falls vacant.
agency.process: It is run by civil servants inside a department, which sets its goals and budget. A minister answers for it.

appointed.label: Board appointed by ministers
appointed.how_often: Members are appointed for fixed terms, usually a few years at a time.
appointed.process: Ministers appoint the chair and board, normally after an open competition that follows the public appointments rules.

company.label: Company owned by government
company.how_often: Directors are appointed by the owner when terms end.
company.process: It is set up like a company. The government (or a public body) owns it and appoints the board.

nhs.label: Board appointed, not elected
nhs.how_often: Board members are appointed for fixed terms.
nhs.process: The chair and board are appointed through the NHS appointments process in its nation. Local people are not asked to vote.

judicial.label: Judges chosen by an independent commission
judicial.how_often: Judges are usually appointed until they retire.
judicial.process: An independent commission picks candidates on merit (in England and Wales, the Judicial Appointments Commission). Judges are not elected, so they can be fair to everyone.

parliament-body.label: Answers to a parliament
parliament-body.how_often: Its leaders are appointed by or with the agreement of the parliament.
parliament-body.process: It works for a parliament (for example, checking how public money is spent) rather than for ministers, so it can be independent of the government.

combined.label: Led by an elected mayor and local council leaders
combined.how_often: The mayor is elected every 4 years.
combined.process: Voters elect the mayor. From the elections after May 2026, they mark a first and a second choice (the supplementary vote); the May 2026 elections still used first past the post. The leaders of the councils in the area sit on its board. Under the 2026 Act it is a 'strategic authority'.

sources.title: English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026
Written statement, 21 May 2026: the supplementary vote returns

charity.label: Run by a board of trustees
charity.how_often: Trustees serve terms set in its own rules.
charity.process: It is a charity or non-profit body with its own trustees, which government partly funds or controls.

local-body.label: Set up or owned by a local council
local-body.how_often: Its managers or board are appointed by the council when posts fall vacant.
local-body.process: ONS counts it as local government because one or more councils control it. The council, whose councillors are elected, appoints who runs it.

central-body.label: Controlled by government
central-body.how_often: Its leaders are appointed by the government that controls it.
central-body.process: ONS counts it as central government because a government department or devolved government controls it. The sources don't say exactly how its leaders are chosen.

pension.label: Pension scheme for public workers
pension.how_often: Its managers or trustees are appointed under the scheme's rules.
pension.process: It pays pensions to people who worked in public services. Its rules say who runs it.

territory.label: Has its own government
territory.how_often: Elections are held under its own laws.
territory.process: It runs most of its own affairs with its own elected law-makers. The UK is responsible for its defence and relations with other countries.

gla.label: Elected mayor and assembly
gla.process: Londoners elect the Mayor of London and the London Assembly, which checks the Mayor's work. The 2026 Act returns mayoral elections to the supplementary vote (a first and a second choice) after May 2026. The Greater London Authority is a mayoral strategic authority under that Act.

sources.title: English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026

unknown.label: Not stated in the sources
unknown.process: The sources don't say how this body is led. You can help by sending a correction.

meta.notes: Purpose and activity are worked out from each body's kind, name and description (modelled). How a body is formed is the rule for its kind, with the law or guidance it comes from. Election facts checked against the Acts on 22 November 2026.
